strengths: Provides the first in-depth mechanistic analysis of unexpected code-switching in LLMs using sparse autoencoders, identifying language-specific features whose pre-activation values rise before code-switching and validating this causally via directional ablation.
Proposes SASFT, a simple and practical auxiliary-loss method for supervised finetuning that requires no inference-time intervention and directly targets language-specific SAE features.
Conducts extensive experiments across five models, three target languages, two training-data sizes, and six multilingual benchmarks, with comparisons to SFT and SFT+GRPO baselines.
Reports consistent reductions in code-switching, often over 50%, with complete elimination in several cases, while generally preserving or improving multilingual benchmark performance.
Includes useful ablations on layer selection, feature selection, and threshold setting, and provides statistical significance testing for the main code-switching comparisons.
Discusses limitations and outlines reasonable future work, including extension to more languages, larger models, DPO/GRPO, and finer-grained thresholds.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited: the SFT data is proprietary and cannot be released, code is not released, and the custom SAEs trained for Qwen models are not described in sufficient detail (architecture, dictionary size, sparsity, reconstruction quality, training data).

Some evaluation results are inconsistent or potentially misleading: percentage reductions are reported from a baseline of 0.00 to 0.00 as -100%, and the large unexplained HumanEval improvement (+17.7) for Llama-3.1-8B raises questions about evaluation variance or benchmark validity.

Several code-switching ratios are very low in absolute terms, and statistical significance is not universal; some comparisons against SFT or SFT+GRPO yield p-values above 0.05, so the claim of consistent superiority is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

Notation and method details are unclear: the auxiliary loss uses α_j with inconsistent indexing, and it is not fully specified how thresholds are estimated per feature/language or why language features are identified via activation values but constrained via pre-activation values.

The experimental setup for Table 1 is ambiguous: it is not clearly stated whether separate models are trained for each target language and how each column’s code-switching ratio is obtained, which complicates interpretation.

Baseline coverage is narrow: only standard SFT and one SFT+GRPO baseline are compared; inference-time SAE ablation is shown as a feasibility study but not included as a full baseline in the main results.

Scope is limited to Chinese, Russian, and Korean, all models are under 9B parameters, and Table 2 reports benchmark preservation only for the Chinese 230k setting, leaving broader generalization unclear.

The method may suppress legitimate target-language features in some contexts; although multilingual benchmarks are mostly preserved, some drops are observed and the mechanism by which target-language generation remains unaffected is not fully analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: unexpected code-switching in multilingual LLMs.
Uses sparse autoencoders to provide mechanistic insight, linking code-switching to unusually high pre-activation values of target-language features and supporting this with ablation experiments.
Proposes SASFT, a simple auxiliary-loss method that avoids inference-time intervention and can be integrated into standard supervised finetuning.
Evaluates on five models and three target languages with two data-size settings and six multilingual benchmarks, including comparisons to SFT and SFT+GRPO.
Includes some useful ablations on layer/feature selection and the choice of pre-activation threshold, plus implementation details and significance testing.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is an incremental application of previously identified language-specific SAE features, adding an auxiliary penalty on pre-activation values during SFT.

Code-switching detection is script-based and can falsely flag Japanese Kanji or Korean Hanja as Chinese; the evaluation data inconsistently includes Japanese while using Han characters as the Chinese-switch cue, potentially invalidating CSW ratios.

Main claim of '>50% reduction in 26 out of 30 cases' is not supported by Table 1: several baseline ratios are already zero or reductions are below 50%, and many reductions are on very small absolute ratios.
Evaluation/procedure may be leaky: the evaluation query set is described as the same as in Section 3.1, and the private SFT data and unreleased code make exact reproduction impossible.
Hyperparameter choices (last two layers, first two features, lambda grid search) may have been tuned on the reported evaluation metric without a clear held-out validation split, risking overfitting.

The SFT+GRPO baseline is weak and likely not a faithful strong comparison to prior work: it uses only 10k training samples, a simple language-consistency reward, and base models rather than the reasoning-model setting from prior work.

The auxiliary loss formulation is ambiguous: alpha_j is not clearly indexed by feature, and using a possibly negative average pre-activation value as a threshold is not well justified and may over-penalize.

Benchmark results show suspiciously large gains (e.g., +17.7 HumanEval) that are unlikely to be caused by reduced code-switching and may indicate training/evaluation confounds; benchmarks are reported for only one training configuration.
Scope is narrow: only three script-distinct target languages, models under 9B, and no Latin-script code-switching; the method requires SAEs for each model/layer, limiting practical applicability.

The SAE-based analysis remains correlational and assumes feature monosemanticity; penalizing language-specific features may have side effects that are not thoroughly examined beyond selected benchmarks.

strengths: The paper provides the first mechanistic analysis of unexpected code-switching in LLMs using sparse autoencoders, showing that pre-activation values of the target-language feature rise before code-switching occurs.

The proposed SASFT method is simple and well-motivated: it adds an auxiliary loss during supervised fine-tuning to keep pre-activation values of irrelevant language features below estimated thresholds, avoiding inference-time intervention.

The empirical evaluation is broad: five models from three families, three target languages, two training-data sizes, and six multilingual benchmarks, with comparisons to standard SFT and a GRPO-based baseline.
SASFT generally outperforms GRPO on code-switching reduction and is more stable across settings, while largely preserving or improving benchmark performance.
The paper includes useful ablations on layer selection, feature selection, and the threshold choice, as well as statistical significance tests for the main code-switching comparisons.
The limitations are acknowledged, including the focus on a few target languages and models under 9B parameters, which helps scope the conclusions.
The writing is clear and the problem is practically relevant for multilingual LLM deployment.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction overclaim that SASFT reduces code-switching by more than 50% consistently, but Table 1 contains several cases with much smaller reductions (e.g., Gemma-2-9B 230k zh: -7%; Llama-3.1-8B 230k zh: -44%, ko: -37%). The claims should be toned down to match the evidence.

Several results report percentage reductions when the baseline code-switching ratio is already 0.00%, where percentage reduction is undefined or misleading. Absolute differences would be more honest and informative.

The evaluation relies on script-based detection (Han, Cyrillic, Hangul), which limits applicability to code-switching between languages that share a script, such as English, Spanish, French, or transliterated text.

Several code-switching ratios are very low (e.g., below 0.5% in some settings), and not all comparisons are statistically significant. Practical significance and robustness across low-rate regimes need clearer discussion.
Reproducibility is limited: the SFT data is proprietary, and code/checkpoints are not released, making it difficult to verify the main claims independently.

Some benchmark improvements are surprisingly large without explanation (e.g., HumanEval +17.70 for Llama-3.1-8B), and benchmark results are not accompanied by significance tests or extensive analysis of why auxiliary regularization should improve code generation.

The method depends on SAE feature identification. For Qwen3 models, the authors train their own SAEs, but details on SAE quality, validation, and robustness of the language-feature selection are not fully reported.
The notation and description of alpha_j in Eq. 8 are somewhat confusing and could be clarified; it is not fully clear whether the threshold is per source language, per feature, or both.

strengths: Provides a novel and well-motivated SAE-based analysis of unexpected code-switching, identifying unusually high pre-activation values of irrelevant language features before switches occur.
Offers bidirectional causal evidence: ablating language-specific features reduces code-switching, while enhancing them induces code-switching, strengthening the mechanistic claim.
Proposes a simple and practical method, SASFT, that adds an auxiliary loss during SFT to regulate language-feature pre-activations, avoiding inference-time intervention and extra inference overhead.
Evaluates on five models across three target languages, two dataset sizes, and several multilingual benchmarks, with additional ablations on layer and feature selection.
Shows substantial code-switching reduction in most settings and often maintains or improves multilingual benchmark performance, outperforming GRPO and a token-probability penalty baseline.
The writing is generally clear, the method is easy to follow, and code/data availability plus detailed hyperparameters support reproducibility for most components.
The paper addresses an important and under-explored practical issue in multilingual LLMs and connects interpretability tools with a concrete mitigation method.
weaknesses: The abstract claims SASFT 'consistently reduces unexpected code-switching by more than 50%,' but several cases in Table 1 fall below 50% reduction (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B Korean 210k: -19%; Qwen3-8B Chinese 210k: -31%, Chinese 110k: -26%). This overclaim should be corrected.

Evaluation is limited to Chinese, Russian, and Korean because the code-switching detector relies on distinct scripts. This excludes code-switching among Latin-script languages and limits the generality of the task and claims; the script-based detector may also produce false positives for names, quotations, or code snippets.

Details of the Qwen3 SAEs are missing: architecture, training corpus, sparsity, dictionary size, and reconstruction quality are not provided. This is important for reproducibility and for assessing whether the method depends on SAE quality.

The baseline comparison is not fully balanced: SFT+GRPO uses only 10k RL samples while SFT/SASFT use 110k or 210k samples, and the SFT+Penalty baseline lacks justification for its penalty coefficient search. No statistical significance or seed variance is reported for the main code-switching and benchmark results.

The notation around the threshold in Eq. (8) is confusing: α_j appears inside a sum over features s in the target-language feature set S_L, but the text describes α_j as associated with feature s in language j. It is unclear whether the threshold is per-feature or per-language, which matters because feature scales differ.

The main experiments use the first two language features from the last two layers, but the layer/feature ablations are not exhaustive across all models, languages, and dataset settings. The paper also lacks controls using random or non-language-specific SAE directions to fully isolate the effect.
The paper inconsistently refers to six benchmarks while listing seven: MMLU, HumanEval, Flores, HellaSwag, LogiQA, IFEval, and MGSM.

Some benchmark degradations are larger than the claimed 'usually within 1-2%' (e.g., Qwen3-8B on Russian 110k shows HumanEval -5.24 and Flores -7.58), so the preservation claim needs more nuanced reporting.
The training overhead and scalability of SASFT with SAE feature extraction during fine-tuning are not analyzed, and all tested models are under 9B parameters, limiting claims about larger LLMs.

The code-switching ratio is coarse: it only indicates whether any target-language script appears, not the frequency or severity of switching, so a single character and an entire switched sentence are treated equally.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: unexpected code-switching in multilingual LLMs, which harms usability and readability.
Provides an interpretability-based analysis using sparse autoencoders and links unexpected code-switching to unusually high pre-activation values of target-language features.
Includes directional ablation and enhancement experiments that offer causal evidence for the relationship between language-specific features and code-switching.
Proposes a simple and reasonably general training-time method, SASFT, that adds an auxiliary regularizer on SAE pre-activations during supervised fine-tuning.
Experiments span five models from three families, three target languages (Chinese, Russian, Korean), two training-data scales, multiple baselines, and six multilingual benchmarks.
Reports substantial code-switching reductions in many settings and provides useful ablations on threshold choice, layer selection, and feature selection.
Shows preliminary robustness of Gemma Scope language-feature identification across some SAE hyperparameter configurations.
weaknesses: Missing or severely under-discussed highly relevant prior work: Nie et al. (2025) already studies mechanistic understanding and mitigation of language confusion, and Wang et al. (2025a) analyzes internal causes of language mixing. The paper claims the only prior solution is Guo et al. (2025), which weakens novelty and positioning.

Main evaluation largely excludes English as a prompt source, even though English is the dominant practical setting and is shown in the motivating examples. The primary code-switching evaluations use Arabic/Thai/Vietnamese/Japanese/Korean prompts, so the paper does not convincingly test the most important English-to-target code-switching scenario.

The GRPO baseline is trained with only 10k samples while SFT and SASFT use 110k or 210k samples. This is an unfair comparison and may explain GRPO's weak and unstable results; the central claim of outperforming GRPO is therefore not well supported.

The claim that SASFT 'consistently outperforms GRPO' is contradicted by Table 1: for Llama-3.1-8B, Korean 210k, GRPO reduces code-switching by 35% while SASFT reduces it by only 19%. Such overclaiming undermines trust in the empirical narrative.

No comparison is made to the original base model before SFT. Benchmark results are reported relative to the SFT baseline, so the paper does not actually demonstrate preservation of original multilingual capabilities, only that SASFT does not degrade relative to SFT.

Several appendix benchmark results show non-trivial degradation, e.g., Flores BLEU drops by 7.58 and HumanEval by 5.24 in some settings, which conflicts with the main-text claim that degradation is 'usually within 1–2%.'
Equation (8) and the threshold notation are unclear: α_j is described inconsistently (per-language vs. per-feature), making the auxiliary loss difficult to reproduce exactly.

For Qwen3 models, the paper trains custom SAEs but provides little detail on SAE training data, architecture, sparsity, reconstruction quality, or feature validation, limiting reproducibility and confidence in those results.

The analysis of language-specific features is primarily demonstrated for Chinese; Russian and Korean analysis is much thinner, and the script-based evaluation cannot handle Latin-script code-switching, restricting generality.
No statistical significance or variance across random seeds is reported; with small code-switching ratios, observed differences may not be robust.
The paper lacks comparisons to simple and strong practical baselines such as explicit prompting ('answer in language X only'), constrained decoding, or logit-bias/ban-token inference-time mitigation.

The method's novelty is incremental relative to Deng et al. (2025): it reuses their language-specific SAE features and applies a fairly straightforward activation regularizer. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its contribution from this prior work.
The submitted manuscript says code and data are 'available at' but provides no actual link or resource information, which further harms reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: unexpected code-switching in multilingual LLMs, which harms usability and reliability.

Provides a mechanistic analysis using sparse autoencoders, linking unexpected code-switching to high pre-activation values of language-specific features, with supporting ablation and enhancement experiments that strengthen causal claims.
Proposes SASFT, a simple and general auxiliary loss that can be added to standard SFT, making the method easy to integrate into existing fine-tuning pipelines.
Extensive empirical evaluation across five models, three target languages, two dataset sizes, and multiple baselines demonstrates consistent reductions in code-switching.
Evaluates multilingual benchmark performance, showing that SASFT generally preserves capabilities and sometimes improves them, which is important for practical adoption.
Includes useful ablations on layer selection, feature selection, and threshold setting, plus appendix robustness checks for SAE configurations.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with limitations and future work discussed.
weaknesses: The abstract claims SASFT reduces unexpected code-switching by more than 50% "consistently," but Table 1 shows many cases below 50% and some only modest improvements; the claims should be softened to match the evidence.
The GRPO baseline is trained with only 10k samples while SFT and SASFT use 110k or 210k samples, making the comparison to the existing GRPO-based method potentially unfair.

Code-switching evaluation lacks statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; ratios are often low and some reported improvements may be within noise, especially since multiple runs are mentioned but not aggregated with variance.

Potential train/test overlap or unclear separation: training data includes Flores and GSM8K-style data, while evaluation uses pm-meval benchmarks including Flores and MGSM, which could affect multilingual benchmark conclusions.

The method notation and thresholding are somewhat confusing: Eq. 8 uses S_L for target-language features but then refers to alpha_j, and the choice of first two features from the last two layers is not fully justified.
Code-switching detection is script-based and limited to Chinese, Russian, and Korean; it cannot handle same-script or romanized code-switching and may miss broader code-switching phenomena.
Some benchmark regressions exist, e.g., Qwen3-8B shows MMLU -2.06 and HellaSwag -2.88, which complicates the claim that SASFT maintains or improves multilingual capabilities.
Reproducibility could be improved: the code/data link appears to be an anonymized placeholder, and details of Qwen SAE training and reliability are not fully described.
Table 1 and Table 3 are unclear about which model is trained on which target language and how the CS columns map to training conditions; this makes the main results harder to interpret.
The paper does not compare against other plausible mitigation strategies such as decoding constraints, prompt-based language control, or language-consistency training at comparable scale.
